strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: Extends RVOS to explicitly model object interactions, which are underexplored in existing datasets and methods
Substantial dataset: InterRVOS-8K with 127K expressions across 8,738 videos is the largest RVOS dataset to date; well-designed 4-stage automatic annotation pipeline
Comprehensive experiments: Thorough ablations (Table 6), zero-shot evaluation across three benchmarks (Table A2), new actor-target-aware evaluation protocol, both quantitative and qualitative results
Strong empirical results: ReVIOSa-1B outperforms larger Sa2VA-4B model (57.9 vs 55.3); consistent improvements across evaluation settings
Clear presentation: Well-written with effective visualizations and transparent dataset statistics; detailed annotation prompts in appendix
weaknesses: Critical: Dataset quality unvalidated - entire 127K dataset is automatically generated with no human evaluation, inter-annotator agreement metrics, or verification of interaction detection accuracy. No discussion of GPT hallucination risks or role assignment correctness despite claiming 'high-quality' annotations

Limited architectural novelty: ReVIOSa is a straightforward application of existing components (SAM2 + InternVL) with two appended special tokens. Interaction modeling reduces to emitting tokens; lacks sophisticated relational reasoning, structured representations, or role-aware attention

Concerning performance pattern: Interaction expressions (65.7, Table 4) significantly underperform appearance+motion (61.0) and appearance-only (59.7), suggesting either poor annotation quality or genuine model struggle with interactions—this is problematic for an 'interaction-aware' task

Narrow evaluation scope: All evaluation on own dataset; no cross-dataset validation on interaction-rich subsets of existing benchmarks; comparisons limited to Sa2VA, Referformer, LMPM; missing recent MLLM baselines

Dataset bias from filtering: Evaluation set uses filtered data to 'increase proportion of interaction-centric expressions,' making it non-representative of training distribution and potentially inflating interaction metrics

Incomplete role analysis: No performance breakdown by interaction type (unidirectional vs. bidirectional), no actor-target confusion pattern analysis, no per-role metrics—unclear how well the model distinguishes roles
Limited interaction diversity: 79.7% of interactions involve 2 objects (Figure A3), mostly simple spatial/contact interactions; no systematic interaction taxonomy or classification
Annotation pipeline robustness unexamined: Accuracy of Stage 3 interaction detection not reported; multi-stage cascading errors not analyzed; potential error propagation across 4 stages not discussed

Incomplete technical specification: Loss function weighting not fully specified (cross-entropy + Dice balance unclear); batch size 2 lacks justification; design choice rationale missing (why tokens vs. structured representations?)

Absence of failure analysis: No systematic investigation of failure modes, role-confusion patterns, problematic interaction types, or sensitivity to design choices; motion-only expressions show particularly poor performance (44.6) without explanation

strengths: Well-motivated problem that identifies a genuine limitation in standard RVOS: the inability to distinguish semantic roles (actor vs. target) in interaction-based expressions
Large-scale InterRVOS-127K dataset (127K expressions) with systematic 4-stage automatic annotation pipeline that is thoroughly documented and reproducible
Comprehensive experimental validation including ablation studies, layer-head selection analysis, zero-shot transfer, and dataset efficiency comparisons that support the proposed approach
Strong zero-shot transfer performance on standard RVOS benchmarks (Table A3) demonstrates that interaction-centric supervision provides robust visual-language grounding beyond the new task
Thorough technical analysis including layer-wise/head-wise attention investigation, attention mask loss justification, and visualization of how AML improves focus on object regions
Qualitative results clearly demonstrate improvements over strong Sa2VA baseline in distinguishing actor and target roles for complex interaction scenarios
weaknesses: Automatic annotation quality is a significant concern: 96% of training data (122,188 expressions) relies on GPT-4o and LLaMA-70B outputs with no explicit quality evaluation metrics, error analysis, or spot-check validation beyond the manually-refined evaluation set

Substantial unexplained performance gap: InterRVOS-Target (67.1-68.3) is 6-7 points lower than InterRVOS-Actor (73.2-75.8), raising questions about task validity and practical utility, yet this gap receives minimal discussion or error analysis

Limited technical novelty: core contributions are straightforward (two special tokens + attention mask loss) with heavy reliance on existing components (InternVL-2.5 MLLM + SAM2). AML improvement is modest (+1.5 in ablation), and no comparison with simpler alternatives is provided

Evaluation protocol lacks clarity for bidirectional interactions: dataset contains significant proportion of symmetric interactions, but how actor-target distinction applies to these cases is not explicitly explained
Limited interaction complexity scope: 80% of interactions involve 2 objects, 20% involve 3. Scalability beyond binary/ternary interactions is not demonstrated or discussed

No downstream task evaluation: paper does not validate whether separate actor-target segmentation actually improves performance on relevant applications (action recognition, interaction understanding), limiting evidence of practical impact

Dataset bias and generalization concerns: dataset is built exclusively from VidOR using automatic generation; potential for distribution bias and systematic errors from LLM outputs is not investigated

Attention Mask Loss design not fully justified: using BCE on patch-level resized masks to supervise continuous attention is a crude approximation; no comparison with alternative loss functions or regularization approaches
